title: Shelter
summary: Pick flat, dry ground out of the wind, insulate from the ground first and keep the shelter small.

list: Flat, dry ground above flood level, with no dead trees or hanging branches overhead.
Avoid low ground such as narrow valleys and creek beds: cold air collects there at night. Pick a spot out of the wind.
Near water and fuel, but never in a dry wash or stream bed: flash floods run there.

Stay out of the path of avalanches and rockslides. In the Adirondacks, avalanche-prone terrain is found on steep, open slopes, slides and gullies on mountains throughout the park, not only in the High Peaks.

blocks.cap: Low ground collects cold air at night and floods. Pick level ground above flood level, out of the wind.

steps: Insulate from the ground first: a bed of dry leaves, grass or boughs at least 12 inches thick, because it packs down when you lie on it. At rest you can lose as much as 80 percent of your body heat to the ground.
Keep it small, just big enough to lie in. A shelter that is too big wastes your body heat.

Debris hut: prop a long ridgepole on a stump or tree at about waist height. Lean sticks along both sides, steep enough to shed rain, then pile leaves and debris at least 3 feet thick, the thicker the better. Pile debris by the entrance that you can pull in to plug it once you're inside.

Lean-to: lash a pole between two trees, lean branches against it with the back of the lean-to into the wind, and cover with boughs or a tarp. Build a fire in front, with a wall of green logs or dry, solid rock behind it to reflect heat in. Never use wet, porous or riverbed rocks: they can explode when heated.
Tarp: tie a line between two trees about waist high and pitch the tarp from it as a lean-to, with its back into the wind.

blocks.cap: Debris hut. Ridgepole at about waist height, debris at least 3 feet thick.
Lean-to. The log wall throws the fire’s heat back into the shelter.

blocks.p: You need a tarp or poncho, 7 to 10 feet (2 to 3 m) of rope or cord, stakes about 1 foot (30 cm) long (three for a poncho) and two trees or poles 7 to 10 feet (2 to 3 m) apart. These are the Army’s figures for a poncho lean-to (Army ATP 3-50.21).

steps: Check the wind before you pick the trees. The back of the lean-to must face into the wind.
Poncho: tie off the hood first. Pull the drawstring tight, roll the hood lengthwise, fold it in thirds and tie it with the drawstring.
Cut the rope in half. Tie one half to each corner of one long edge of the tarp. This edge is the high front edge.

Tie a drip stick, about 4 inches (10 cm) long, to each rope about 1 inch (2.5 cm) from the tarp. Rain running along the rope drips off the stick instead of into the shelter. Strings about 4 inches (10 cm) long tied to the grommets along the high edge help the water run off the same way.

Tie each rope to its tree about waist high, so the high edge is stretched between the trees. The ropes and the tarp’s high edge are the line between two trees in Build above: you don’t need a separate line.

Spread the tarp down toward the wind and stake its other long edge to the ground with sharpened sticks through the grommets. The low, staked edge is the back of the lean-to, facing into the wind. The open side, under the high edge, faces away from it.

Staying more than one night, or rain coming? Hold up the middle. Poncho: tie a line from the hood to an overhanging branch, with no slack. Any tarp: stand a stick upright under the center (it takes up room inside).
Pile brush, a pack or other gear at the sides of the lean-to for more shelter from wind and rain.
Put leaves or pine needles inside to lie on, to cut heat loss to the ground (see Build).

blocks.cap: Tarp lean-to. The ropes hold the high front edge between the trees; the low back edge is staked down, into the wind.

blocks.p: For tying the ropes, see Knots.

It takes longer than a tarp lean-to but needs no tools, or only a knife. You need two trees or upright poles about 7 feet (2 m) apart, one pole about 7 feet (2 m) long and 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick, five to eight poles about 10 feet (3 m) long and 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick, cord or vines, and saplings or vines to weave across (Army ATP 3-50.21).

steps: Tie the 7-foot pole across the two trees at waist to chest height. No trees? Hold it up with Y-shaped sticks or two tripods.
Lean the 10-foot poles against it, all on one side. That side is the back of the lean-to: it faces into the wind.
Weave saplings or vines across the poles.
Cover the frame with brush, leaves, pine needles or grass, starting at the bottom and working up, like shingles.
Put straw, leaves, pine needles or grass inside for bedding.

blocks.p: In cold weather, build a reflector wall behind the fire in front of the lean-to (Army ATP 3-50.21): see Fire, Reflectors.

list: Instead of a stump or tree, you can hold up the ridgepole with a tripod: two short stakes and the ridgepole (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Make the ribbing wide enough for your body (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Lay finer sticks and brush crosswise over the ribs. This lattice keeps the leaves and needles from falling through onto you (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Use light, dry, soft debris such as grass, pine needles and leaves (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Inside, lay insulation 2 feet (60 cm) thick to lie on (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Finish with branches on top of the debris so wind doesn’t blow it away (Army ATP 3-50.21).
Snow insulates well, so a snow cave or snow trench can keep you alive. Make a ventilation hole in the roof and build the sleeping platform higher than the entrance.

Never use a charcoal grill, lantern or portable camping stove inside a tent or snow shelter, and never use fuel-burning heaters or lanterns while sleeping in one. Carbon monoxide kills people every year this way.

blocks.cap: Snow trench with a vent hole. Sleep on a raised shelf: cold air sinks to the low end.

blocks.p: The quickest snow shelter to build (US Antarctic Program; Army TC 21-3).

steps: Dig a trench about 3 feet (1 m) deep and as wide as your shoulders, long enough to lie down in with room for your gear (US Antarctic Program).

Roof it with a tarp or poncho held down with snow blocks, stakes, a shovel or other gear (US Antarctic Program). In firm snow you can cut blocks and lean them against each other across the top instead (Army FM 21-76, TC 21-3). Skis, poles or snowshoes laid across can hold up the roof (Army TC 21-3).
Make only one entrance, and close it with a snow block or your pack (Army FM 21-76).
Lay boughs over the roof and for your bed, and insulate under you (Army TC 21-3; see Build).
Leave a ventilation hole in the roof (see Snow, above).

blocks.p: For two people, widen the bottom into a bell shape, but keep the opening at the top shoulder-wide (US Antarctic Program).

A snow cave takes time and energy, and you will get wet digging it from sweat and snow (Army ATP 3-50.21, TC 21-3). Dig in as little clothing as you can, so you have dry clothes to change into when you finish (Army TC 21-3).

steps: Find a drift at least 10 feet (3 m) deep. Don’t use newly fallen, powdery or loose snow (Army TC 21-3, ATP 3-50.21).

Put the entrance about 45 degrees from the downwind side. Dig a small tunnel straight into the drift about 3 feet (1 m), then dig out the room to the left and right, so it runs crosswise to the tunnel (Army TC 21-3).

Make the sleeping platform higher than the top of the entrance, where the air is warmer (Army TC 21-3, ATP 3-50.21). Dig a small trench between the platform and the wall so melting snow doesn’t wet you and your gear (Army ATP 3-50.21).

Arch the roof so it is strong and drips run down the walls instead of onto you. Keep the walls and roof at least 1 foot (30 cm) thick, and high enough to sit up on the platform (Army ATP 3-50.21, TC 21-3).
Make at least two vent holes, one in the roof and one in the door (Army TC 21-3). Check them every 2 or 3 hours for snow or ice, and clear them from inside with a pole or stick (Army TC 21-3).
Block the entrance with a pack, poncho or snow block when you’re not using it (Army TC 21-3, ATP 3-50.21).
Mark the entrance outside with skis or other gear stood upright (Army TC 21-3).

list: Don’t walk on the roof: it can collapse (Army TC 21-3).
If you can’t see your breath inside, it’s too warm: cool it down before the roof melts and drips (Army ATP 3-50.21).

blocks.p: No drift deep enough for a snow cave? Pile snow into a mound and dig it out (Army ATP 3-50.21). The sizes here come from Scout Life (Boy Scouts of America) and the Appalachian Mountain Club; no agency source opened gives them.

steps: Shovel snow into a mound at least 5 feet (1.5 m) high, ideally 7 to 8 feet (2.1 to 2.4 m), and wide enough to hold everyone who will sleep in it once it’s hollowed out (Appalachian Mountain Club; Scout Life).

Shape it into a dome and let it settle about 90 minutes so the snow bonds together (Scout Life; the Appalachian Mountain Club says 60 to 90 minutes in most conditions). Very cold, granular snow takes longer and may not bond at all. Test it first: if a snowball won’t hold together, don’t build a quinzhee from that snow (Appalachian Mountain Club).
Push sticks a foot (30 cm) deep into the mound all over, from the outside (Appalachian Mountain Club).

Dig a small entrance at the base on the downwind side, just big enough to crawl through (Appalachian Mountain Club; Scout Life says the downhill side). Hollow out the inside. Stop wherever you reach the end of a stick, so the walls stay at least 1 foot (30 cm) thick (Appalachian Mountain Club; Scout Life: 1 to 2 feet). If you can see light through a wall, it’s too thin (Appalachian Mountain Club). Don’t dig through a wall.
Poke a small ventilation hole near the top of the dome (Scout Life).
Leave the last foot of snow as raised beds, and dig a narrow trench between them down to the ground so cold air drains out (Scout Life).
Mark the entrance, keep a small shovel inside in case you have to dig your way out, and change into warm, dry clothes once it’s built (Scout Life).

blocks.cap: Quinzhee cut in half. Stop digging wherever you reach the end of a stick. Leave a ventilation hole near the top, and raised beds with a trench between them so cold air drains out.

sections.h: Fire and stoves in and near shelters

blocks.warn: Never use a charcoal grill, lantern or portable camping stove inside a tent or snow shelter, and never use fuel-burning heaters or lanterns while sleeping in one (CDC, CPSC). Some Army cold-weather manuals heat snow caves with stoves or candles, or cook in the entrance. This app doesn’t: it follows CDC and CPSC.

list: No fire, candle, fuel gel or oil lamp inside a tent or snow shelter either: candles, fuel gel and small oil lamps make carbon monoxide (Army ATP 3-50.21), and CDC says not to burn anything in a stove or fireplace that isn’t vented (see Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors).
Heat melts a snow shelter: it melts the snow that insulates you, and melting snow overhead can soak you and bury you and your gear (Army FM 21-76).
Keep a fire in front of a lean-to from burning too hot and burning the shelter down (Army TC 21-3).
People trying to get warm or dry clothes by a fire get careless and scorch or burn their clothes and gear (Army FM 21-76).

Never leave a fire unattended, and asleep counts as unattended: if the fire in front of a lean-to must burn while people sleep, one person stays awake to watch it; otherwise put it out before you sleep (Army TC 21-3 gives this rule for snow caves in severe weather; this app applies it to a lean-to fire; Fire).

sources.name: Appalachian Mountain Club, How to Build a Quinzee (aka Snow Cave) (Matt Heid, March 28, 2015)
sources.used: Snowball test (snow that crumbles is not suitable); pile at least five feet, ideally seven to eight feet high; bonds in 60 to 90 minutes in most conditions, wet snow just below freezing quickly, granular snow at low temperatures takes longer and may not bond at all; sticks a foot deep from outside; walls at least a foot thick, light through the wall means too thin; small entrance at the base, on the downwind side; don't dig through the wall
